newsitem.title: JAPAN: Greenpeace urges Japan initiative on CO2 emissions.
newsitem.headline: Greenpeace urges Japan initiative on CO2 emissions.

text.p: Environmental watchdog Greenpeace accused Japan of failing to grapple with the issue of global warming caused by burning fossil fuels despite its role as next year's host to an international conference on climatic changes.
Bill Hare, a policy director at Greenpeace, said in an interview that Japan appeared worried that moves to curb greenhouse gases would hamper economic growth.
"I think the Japanese government is unusually pessimistic about the implications...(that) reducing carbon dioxide emissions (might have on the economy)," Hare said.

In a declaration in July, the industrial powers agreed to push for an accord on "quantified, legally binding objectives for emission limitations" to be finalised at a Climate Change Conference in Kyoto in December 1997.

The declaration said it would press for "significant reductions", and that measures to achieve this would cover a wide variety of industries where oil and coal are presently the prime source of energy, including transport, agriculture and forestry.

Hare, who was in Japan to speak at a business seminar on global warming and also to lobby the Japanese government, met officials from several Japanese ministries, including the Foreign Ministry, the Ministry of International Trade and Industry and the Environment Agency.
The Trade Ministry, in particular, seemed worried about the possible damaging impact curbs on greenhouse gases would have on economic growth, he said.

Scientists widely believe man-made carbon emissions, produced by the use of oil and coal, have a damaging effect on the earth's climate and should be cut in order to prevent a range of crises, including massive floods and hurricanes.
According to local newspaper reports, Japan has drafted proposals for the climate convention that suggest countries be given a choice on how to set targets to reduce CO2 emissions.
One option would be to set emission goals based on the amount of carbon dioxide emissions per capita. A second option would cut CO2 emission levels by a set percentage vis-a-vis 1990 levels.
A government official, who declined to be named, denied the newspaper report. He said Japan's proposal had not yet been finalised and negotiations were still taking place.
He acknowledged, however, that offering a variety of choices provided a possible solution on reaching an agreement as countries currently differ widely in the volume of carbon dioxide they emit.
Hare said that if the newspaper reports were true he was disappointed as they show Japan was not ready to make any emission reductions at all.
"The positions are very much like the position Japan put forward in the middle of 1991, five years ago," he said. "I'm astonished things haven't moved much further," he said.
"A per capita emission target doesn't make any sense at all because it would allow emissions to grow on absolute terms."
Hare said the United States might put forward a goal of a 10 percent reduction in volume by 2010 compared to 1990, and the European Union a 10 percent reduction by 2005.
The government source said economic growth could not be totally forfeited to combat global warming.
"We need a balance between fighting global warming and economic growth," he said. "Japan wants to propose a plan that would be widely accepted," the source said.
"As the host country Japan has responsibility in the outcome of the talks, however we do not want to set a target too far out of reach," he said.
